entries.title: Who is a 'consumer'
entries.summary: A person who buys goods or hires/avails services for a price (paid, promised or partly paid), including offline or online transactions through electronic means. It excludes people who buy for resale or for a commercial purpose.

entries.title: Deficiency in service
entries.summary: Any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance of a service, including negligence or omission that causes loss, and deliberately withholding relevant information.

entries.title: Unfair trade practice (incl. refusing returns/refunds)
entries.summary: Includes deceptive or unfair selling methods, and specifically refusing, after selling goods or providing a service, to take back defective goods, withdraw deficient services, or refund the price within the period stated in the bill/receipt - or within 30 days if no period is stated.

entries.title: Where to file a consumer complaint
entries.summary: A complaint can be filed in the District Commission where the opposite party lives/does business, where the cause of action arose, OR where the complainant lives or personally works for gain.

entries.title: Filing a complaint before the District Commission
entries.summary: The consumer (or a recognised consumer association, or a group of consumers with permission) can file a complaint about defective goods, deficient services or unfair trade practices. The complaint may be filed electronically. The Act does not require you to hire a lawyer.

entries.law: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021
entries.title: Which Commission (by amount paid)
entries.summary: Decided by the value of goods/services PAID as consideration: up to Rs 50 lakh -> District Commission; above Rs 50 lakh up to Rs 2 crore -> State Commission; above Rs 2 crore -> National Commission (NCDRC).

entries.title: Time limit for consumer complaints
entries.summary: A complaint must be filed within 2 years from the date the cause of action arose. A later complaint can be admitted only if the Commission accepts there was sufficient cause for the delay (and records reasons).

entries.law: Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2020
entries.title: Filing fee
entries.summary: No fee for complaints where the value of goods/services paid is up to Rs 5 lakh. Above that, fees rise in slabs - check the current table on e-Jagriti before filing.

entries.title: E-commerce grievance officer
entries.summary: Every e-commerce entity must have a grievance officer whose name and contact are shown on its platform. The officer must acknowledge a consumer complaint within 48 hours and resolve it within one month of receiving it.

entries.title: Online filing: e-Jagriti
entries.summary: Consumer complaints to District, State and National Commissions are filed online at e-jagriti.gov.in (it replaced the older e-Daakhil portal from January 2025): register, fill in details, upload documents, pay the fee if any.

entries.title: National Consumer Helpline (free, pre-litigation)
entries.summary: Free route before going to a Commission: call 1915 or register at consumerhelpline.gov.in / the NCH app. NCH takes up the grievance with the company; many refunds get resolved here.

entries.title: Compensation for breach of contract
entries.summary: When a contract is broken, the party who suffers can claim compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach (or that both sides knew was likely), but not for remote and indirect loss.

entries.title: Time limit for a civil money-recovery suit
entries.summary: A civil suit to recover money such as a security deposit generally has to be filed within 3 years. Which Article applies, and the exact start date (when the refund fell due, or when it was refused), depends on the facts - confirm with a lawyer if you are close to 3 years.

entries.title: Notice before suing the Government
entries.summary: Before filing a civil suit against the Government or a public officer (for official acts), a written notice must be delivered and 2 months must pass (unless the court gives leave to sue earlier).

entries.title: Security deposit cap (only where a State has adopted the Model Tenancy Act)
entries.summary: Caps the security deposit at 2 months' rent for residential premises (6 months for non-residential); it is refundable when the tenant hands back the premises, after deducting the tenant's dues. It is a MODEL law: it applies only in States that passed a law based on it.

entries.law: State rent laws + the rent agreement
entries.title: Deposit rules depend on your State and your agreement
entries.summary: Rent/tenancy law is State-specific. In most everyday cases the deposit refund is governed by what the rent / leave-and-licence agreement says; keeping the deposit without a valid deduction is a breach of that agreement.

entries.title: Deadline for paying wages
entries.summary: Monthly wages must be paid before the end of the 7th day of the following month. If an employee is removed, dismissed, retrenched or resigns, the wages due must be paid within 2 working days. (The Code on Wages came into force on 21 Nov 2025, replacing older wage laws.)

entries.title: Claim for unpaid wages before the wage authority
entries.summary: An employee (or their registered trade union, or the Inspector-cum-Facilitator) can apply to the authority appointed by the government for unpaid or delayed wages. File within 3 years (later only with sufficient cause). The authority can order payment plus compensation of up to 10 times the amount.

entries.title: Cheque bounce
entries.summary: If a cheque given for a debt bounces, the payee must send a written demand notice within 30 days of getting the bank's return memo; the drawer then has 15 days from receiving the notice to pay. If not paid, the payee can file a criminal complaint within one month after that (s.142). It is a criminal case - get a lawyer.
verified_by: https://www.advocatekhoj.com/library/bareacts/negotiableinstruments/138.php (15-day text shown is pre-2003; 30 days per Act 55 of 2002)

entries.title: What a legal notice is
entries.summary: A formal written demand sent before going to court. For most private disputes it is not legally required (exceptions include suits against the Government under CPC s.80 and cheque bounce under NI Act s.138), but it creates a dated record, often triggers payment, and is useful evidence later. You can send it yourself by Registered Post with AD / Speed Post and keep the receipt.

entries.title: Replying to a notice you received
entries.summary: A private legal notice from the other side is a demand, not a court order. Replying puts your side on record. Court summons, police notices and government notices are different - they carry binding dates, so get a lawyer.

entries.title: Criminal breach of trust (replaced IPC 405-409)
entries.summary: Dishonestly misusing property that was entrusted to someone. Ordinary non-payment of a deposit or salary is usually treated as a civil dispute; a criminal complaint fits only where there is dishonest misappropriation. Talk to a lawyer before going the criminal route.

entries.title: Cheating (replaced IPC 415-420)
entries.summary: Deceiving someone dishonestly to make them hand over property. Courts require a dishonest intention from the very start (e.g. a fake seller who never meant to deliver) - not just a late refund.

entries.title: FIR / Zero FIR (replaced CrPC 154)
entries.summary: Information about a cognizable offence can be given at any police station, irrespective of where the offence happened (Zero FIR), including by electronic communication (sign within 3 days). The informant gets a free copy.

entries.title: Screenshots, chats, recordings as evidence (replaced Evidence Act s.65B)
entries.summary: Electronic records (WhatsApp chats, emails, screenshots, audio) can be used as evidence with a certificate about the device/source. Keep the ORIGINAL phone/file safe - not just forwarded copies.

entries.title: Who gets a free lawyer
entries.summary: Free legal services for: SC/ST members, victims of trafficking or forced labour, women and children, persons with disability, victims of disasters/ethnic violence/caste atrocity, industrial workmen, people in custody, and people with income below the limit set by the government.

entries.title: Free legal help: NALSA 15100 / District Legal Services Authority
entries.summary: Call 15100 (NALSA's free legal-aid helpline) or visit the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at your district court for free advice, a free lawyer if eligible, and Lok Adalat settlement.
